What did we do before 40 hours of labor a week? We grew food. We looked at and studied the stars. We raised our children. We cared for our village. We made art. We danced. We cried. We truly lived and loved.

There are many more jobs that humans will still need to do, despite the claims only 5 jobs will survive. AI is not capable of complex analysis of a problem solving nature ranging from engineering, construction, medicine, scientific research or drugs testing to name just 5 areas that will have next to no AI involved other than for repetitive processes. AI will work well in laboratory style conditions in warehouses and for high functioning repetition that doesn't require much interaction such as computer interaction in order to provide a natural language interface for queries put by those with internet access and an ability to phrase questions or commands in such a way as to reduce ambiguity to a low risk of failure. As AI is only as good as the data it has access to, then clearly, there's left space for bad actors to screw up any half decent progress made. In all sincerity, you have to question whether or not the books being uploaded into data centres to enhance AI access to a broader base of information, even if a book is non-fiction, there's no guarantee that the content will be truthful or even remotely accurate. So the rich want to get richer but the models have been found wanting. I think I know where it will all end but I won't discuss these thoughts online. Needless to say, we will need to start thinking about failsafe backup systems and not rely too heavily on others keeping integrity of the data. I'll leave you to ponder as to why this will be necessary to preserve what we know when our generations have long since faded away and many new generations haven't been taught the beauty of hunting for a good read and to have the authors clued up way of writing about subjects you may wish to read about in the future but no longer have access to books.

AI nie zastąpi w pełni księgowych, ale mocno zmieni sposób ich pracy. Zastąpi najżmudniejszą część ich pracy - wprowadzanie i przepisywanie danych między systemami sprzedażowymi (faktury), maile i księgowymi. Jak w każdej pracy umysłowej odpadną proste, żmudne zadania, a te trudne decyzyjne pozostaną. Faktury ustrukturyzowane w XML mogły być już lata temu - KSEF jest dobrym kierunkiem, tylko jego realizacja jest bez sensu - nie przetestowany, prawdopodbnie źle zaprojektowany w pewnych częściach. Problemem od zawsze jest integracja przepływu danych między systemami - między przedsiębiorstwami, między przedsiębiorstwami a urzędami, między działami w firmach (silosy). Jak już KSEF okrzepnie, to będzie potrzebne bardzo mocne uproszczenie prawa podatkowego, które czasami jest sprzeczne lub uznaniowe (nie wiadomo jaka stawka VAT na dany produkt lub usługę - patrz pączki). Lata temu było zabronione (przez urzędników) wysyłanie maili PDFami. Były legendy miejskie, że fakturę z maila po wydrukowaniu trzeba było pozginać i podpisać długopisem - by urzędnik w trakcie kontroli się nie czepiał, że to nie jest oryginał. Po latach wprowadzono ustawę, że faktura może być bez podpisu i przesyłana mailem czy udostępniana w systemie. Teraz nie wolno wysłać kontrahentowi z Polski faktury w PDF poza KSEF, bo urząd skarbowy (KAS) twierdzi, że to druga faktura (mimo tego samego numeru, daty wystawienia, wartości i zawartości pozycji na fakturze) i potrzeba drugi raz od niej VAT zapłacić. Patologią są urzędnicy i biurokracja. O ile więcej polscy przedsiębiorcy mogli by osiągnąć, gdyby nie mieli rzucanych kłód pod nogi przez urzędników, biurokrację i chore przepisy. A i tak jako gospodarka, naród i państwo radzimy sobie bardzo dobrze w Europie - jeszcze nam się chce. Po angielsku są osobne terminy na księowych: bookkeeper i accountant - mniej będzie potrzeba tych pierwszych, więcej tych drugich. Tak, jak w programowaniu potrzeba mniej koderów (klepaczy kodu), tak samo w księgowości będzie potrzeba mniej przepisywaczy danych z papieru do systemów, a więcej myślących księgowych i optymalizujących koszty. Dobry księgowy jest również doradcą dla przedsiębiorcy - czasami realizuje również część zadań dyrektorów finansowych. To my ludzie (mentalnie i nawykowo) ograniczamy rozwój technologii takich jak, robotyka, software, atom, samochody elektryczne. Postęp i rozwój technologiczny mógłby być dużo szybszy. W Chinach robotyzacja i latające drony osobowe (taksówki) będą za chwilę. Już Ford ponad 100 lat temu mówił coś w stylu: "Gdybym zapytał ludzi czego potrzebują, to odpowiadali by najczęściej, że szybszych koni". My nie potrzebujemy mniej księgowych, tylko prostszych przepisów podatkowych. To się nie wydarzy, bo skomplikowane i rozbudowane systemy prawne: 1. utrzymują armię biurokratów i prawników (oraz doradców podatkowych), 2. pozwalają na wykorzystywanie luk prawnych wybranym "dobrze poinformowanym" lub wielkim (nieuczciwa przewaga konkurencyjna). 3. utrudniają odnajdywanie nieprawidłowości - czyli przestępców działających nielegalnie.

Świetny risercz, czytelny podział treści, idealne tempo, bezbłędny język, a przede wszystkim niemal niespotykana już rzetelność. Ten kanał jest oślepiająco jasną perłą polskiego YouTube i aż żal ściska, że film ma pół tysiąca, a nie pół miliona polubień. Co do samej technologii, ostatnio próbowałem korzystać z usług GPT5 i muszę przyznać, że w mojej pracy wciąż nie nadaje się on nawet na asystenta. Model nie potrafi odróżnić informacji źródłowych od swoich halucynacji. Nabrałem pewności, że będzie tak dopóty, dopóki nie będzie rozumiał znaczenia pojęć, którymi się posługuje. Ale żeby je zrozumiał, musielibyśmy nauczyć go świata. Człowiek postrzega rzeczywistość zmysłami, a pojęcia, które stworzył, oddają sposób, w jaki ludzki mózg ją interpretuje i porządkuje byty. Trzeba by na dobry początek nakarmić AI miriadami trójwymiarowych modeli każdego z tych bytów, żeby maszynowo nauczyć ją, czym są (skoro nie potrafimy zreplikować sposobu, w jaki nasz mózg uczy się pojedynczymi krokami zamiast tysięcy powtórzeń). Kłania się jednak de Saussure i pytanie, ile pojęć można zrozumieć bez rozumienia większej struktury, np. doznań czerpanych poprzez inne zmysły niż budujący przestrzenne modele zmysł wzroku. Może jednak taka sieć neuronowa, uczona przez niezliczonych tatusiów i mamusie, mogłaby od poziomu niemowlęcia stopniowo przejść do poziomu dorosłego uczonego korzystającego z monstrualnej bazy danych, tylko że ten proces dojrzewania do etapu AI jako wiarygodnego źródła wiedzy wymagałby wielu lat pracy. Tymczasem twórcy tej technologii idą na skróty. Większa moc obliczeniowa, więcej połączeń, optymalizacja tego czy innego procesu i snucie bajd o nieograniczonych możliwościach modelu, który już zaraz za sprawą "osobliwości" jak za dotknięciem magicznej różdżki stanie się samoświadomym geniuszem to wszystko działania ewidentnie napędzane potrzebami biznesowymi. Oczywiście dla większości ludzi, którzy nie mieszczą się w kategorii potencjalnych klientów big techu jest to narracja przerażająca. Mnie jednak wciąż bardziej od sztucznej inteligencji przeraża sztuczna głupota i jej potencjalny wpływ na człowieka.

To tak jak z radiem Erewań: nie za dwa lata ale za 15 - 20 i nie twór marketingowy zwany sztuczną inteligencją ale realne procesy automatyzacji i cyfryzacji i ich wpływ na kulturę i efektywność. 1. Środowisko Zamknięte vs. Otwarte Autor filmu popełnił błąd logiczny, zrównując drogę publiczną z salą operacyjną. Droga (Chaos): Na drodze masz pijanych kierowców, dzieci wbiegające pod koła, zmienną pogodę i miliony nieprzewidywalnych bodźców. To jest środowisko "brudne". Sala Operacyjna / Tor F1 (Laboratorium): To są środowiska skrajnie kontrolowane. Na torze F1 nie ma kałuż z nienacka ani krów na środku drogi. Wewnątrz ciała pacjenta panują określone warunki anatomiczne. AI nie musi "uważać na przechodniów" – musi optymalizować ruchy skalpela na podstawie mapy tkanek. 2. Precyzja poza zasięgiem biologii Chirurg, nawet wybitny, ma swoje ograniczenia: drżenie rąk (tremor), zmęczenie po 10 godzinach pracy, ograniczone pole widzenia. Merytorycznie: Roboty takie jak Da Vinci już teraz są sterowane przez ludzi, ale ich wersje autonomiczne (np. STAR – Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot) już w testach na tkankach miękkich wykonywały szycie lepiej i precyzyjniej niż ludzie. Jeśli włożymy w to algorytmy nowej generacji, to AI nie będzie "naśladować" chirurga – ona go ośmieszy swoją stabilnością i tempem reakcji. 2–3 lata na wdrożenie w wyspecjalizowanych placówkach to termin bardzo realny technicznie. 3. Bariera jest mentalna, nie techniczna To, co autor filmu wziął za "brak technologii", to w rzeczywistości brak akceptacji prawnej i społecznej. Bolid F1 prowadzony przez AI już dzisiaj wykręciłby rekordy toru, których żaden człowiek by nie przeżył ze względu na przeciążenia. Problem w tym, że nikt nie chce oglądać wyścigu robotów – chcemy oglądać dramat człowieka. W chirurgii jest odwrotnie: nie chcemy "dramatu", chcemy 100% skuteczności. Dlatego parcie na autonomię w medycynie będzie ogromne.

AI is not replacing human thinking; it is replacing large portions of human search and recall. It acts as a compression layer over collective knowledge, helping us jump directly to high probability ideas, solutions, and designs. The gain is speed. The cost is visibility into the reasoning trail. Humans often remember not only what decision was made, but why it was made, what alternatives were rejected, and what constraints shaped the outcome. AI can frequently reconstruct the destination, but it may not preserve the journey. The risk of widespread AI adoption is therefore not the loss of answers, but the gradual erosion of understanding. We become better at reaching conclusions and worse at remembering the causal chains that justified them. In that sense, AI is best viewed as an amplifier of human cognition, not a substitute for it.

On the topic of AI making art: we risk confusing the artistic process with the artifact it produces. The artistic process is ALL about the struggle and the friction. Remove that with AI, and you skip the process by going straight to the artifact. When I make art (paint, write music), what I care about is the process, how it changes me as artist. As much as I like AI for other things, I have no desire to give up the most meaningful part of the process, no matter how cool the AI is. So, as a rule, when I just care about the artifact, which is not too often e.g. background music for a podcast intro, I am OK using AI (the concern of how that AI has been trained, with whose material, with whose permission, is a separate matter). When I care about the process, I don't use AI. Not because it's cheating on an external rule that says "you shall not use AI", but rather because it defeats the purpose of making art.

When it comes to clients where the domain for which the developer is coding is specific (90% of projects), AI doesn't move past basic tasks: comments and unit tests (and even those are very often in need of correction). The nature of the work has changed; there’s a huge saving on boilerplate, but it’s definitely not the case that AI writes high-quality, production-ready code, and there’s no indication that it will. Non-developer is certainly not capable of preparing proper context for the AI; to do it right, they’d have to be... a developer themselves. Regardless of the above, it’s sometimes sad to hear what most people think of developers: that they’re just someone who bangs away at a keyboard. Jeśli chodzi o kasjerów to na zachodzie wiele dyskontów rezygnuje z kas automatycznych. Klienci nie umieją ich obsługiwać, potrzebują pomocy, kradną, deklarują zakup innego towaru do ważenia niż rzeczywiście mają w torbach. Ktos musi obsługiwać system monitoringu w takich sklepach gdzie na zachodzie bardzo często nie ma kamer bo nie było takiej potrzeby. Ja bym bardziej powiedział, że rozwój technologii utrzyma miejsca pracy, a mało tego zwiększy zapotrzebowanie na nowe. Szeregowi pracownicy bankow powinni się bać, tak samo telemarketerzy, czy programiści juniorzy albo zbieracze owoców na plantacjach (to ostatnie raczej z braku chętnych do tej pracy w efekcie czego automatyzacji). Bo co z tego, że wprowadzimy kilka autonomicznych ciężarówek na długie trasy jak nie zaparkują same, nie podjada pod rampę, zawiesza się i będą wymagały obsługi, a z drugiej strony będą tak drogie że kierowca będzie wyborem numer 1. Skomplikowane zadania są zbyt drogie w realizacji i bez dofinansowania nie opłacalne. Ogólnie wszystko w filmie zostało powiedziane. The one piece of advice I can give you in regards to maintaining code quality in a world where code reviews are no longer possible is to force the AI agents to write using primarily pure functions, such that >90% of the code has no state or side effects whatsoever, and the ~5% of the code with state and side effects is lifted to the top. All of your code now becomes trivial to understand. Trying to do this with multi paradigm languages (e.g. TypeScript) is quite difficult as it will go against the majority of the AI model's training for that language. However, it can be done by enforcing functional linting rules to force FP in the small, combined with automated AI code reviews to force FP in the large; i.e. using an AI agent tasked to fail codebases with >~5% efffectful code, or codebases where that effectful code has not all been lifted to the top, or where there are functions which are not as small and as generic as possible. If you allow the agent to code in a purely functional programming language, however, then you don't need anywhere near as much tooling to make it write good functional code, because its training data for that language will primarily be well written functional code anyway, and so you're starting in a much better place and are less reliant on tooling to steer it.

4:16 - This is a bit of a catch-22. Part of our jobs as engineers is to validate the output from an AI to make sure we understand exactly what we're shipping to prod so we don't expose things like PII, secrets, security vulnerabilities, performance bottlenecks, etc. The proper way to do that is to have engineers that _understand_ how software is built, and have the skills to actually write clean, secure, performant code. Can an experienced engineer write a narrative or specification clean enough to achieve that end with an agent? Sure. Can younger, less experienced engineers do that? I'm unconvinced. And even if they do develop the skills to write super-specific context narratives, will they have the skills to validate the output generated before shipping to production? Will they catch Big 0 problems before they cause system issues in prod? Good engineers can be trained (and are likely already learning how) to use prompt-engineering to get to similar results in less time while still having the necessary skills to validate the output, however that's achieved. If you're hiring engineers, I'd argue you have to consider both sides of the agentic equation.

Real symptoms, wrong layer. The issue isn’t that AI “doesn’t have context” in general. LLMs have plenty of generic product and code context. The problem is that they don’t automatically have the *right local context* for this system, this architecture, this failure mode, this user flow, or this operational constraint. The fix also isn’t “humans write better prompts” or “seniors review more AI code.” If seniors are drowning in giant AI PRs, the workflow already failed upstream. The real problem is project coherence over time. Agents can generate locally reasonable code faster than teams can verify whether those changes still fit the larger system. So the work isn’t just moving from coding to supervision. It’s moving toward an operating model that preserves intent: clear arcs/phases, explicit design decisions, system docs, contracts, integration tests, review checkpoints, incident/runbook memory, and a way to retrieve the right context at the right time. AI doesn’t remove the need for software process. It makes missing process visible.

But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed. This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output. Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: - AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically. - Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake. - Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed. - Universal basic compute. If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

I am an AI researcher, as well as a researcher in other areas of Electrical Engineering. The example mentioned below, involving a German engineering company struggling with technical translations, reflects a broader pattern I have been observing: many professionals are not yet using AI tools in the way they are actually meant to be used. It is unrealistic to expect that feeding an entire technical manual into an AI system will yield a high-quality, reliable translation. At the same time, it is equally unrealistic today to propose translating such material entirely without AI assistance. The real opportunity lies somewhere in between, and this is where many professionals are currently underestimating their own value. What is missing is a shift in positioning. Rather than competing with AI, you should be presenting your work as that of a consultant and supervisor of technical quality. This is not a speculative idea, but a practical and increasingly necessary reframing of the profession. Your role becomes one of overseeing, validating, and refining AI-generated translations, ensuring that terminology, consistency, and domain-specific nuances are handled correctly. In this context, you could position yourself as a specialist in quality assurance for highly technical translations, responsible for auditing and correcting outputs generated by AI systems. This alone already constitutes a valuable and defensible service. Beyond that, there is a clear opportunity to leverage your expertise more systematically by developing your own tailored tools. Frameworks such as LangGraph or SDKs from OpenAI and Anthropic allow you to build agents that replicate parts of your own review process. You can encode the checks you typically perform, standardize terminology validation, and reduce both fatigue and the risk of human error. Importantly, these agents should not merely generate translations, but also flag uncertainty. For instance, they can be designed to identify segments where terminology is ambiguous, where multiple interpretations are possible, or where the model shows low confidence. These signals can guide your attention toward the parts of the text that genuinely require expert intervention. For the most delicate or high-stakes sections, manual review and correction remain essential. This hybrid approach allows you to focus your effort where it has the highest impact, rather than expending equal effort across the entire document. Ultimately, the service that needs to be offered today is not “human translation” or “AI translation” in isolation, but an integrated workflow that combines both. It is precisely the combination of your accumulated expertise with the scalability of AI that creates value. At the same time, this requires a shift in mindset from both professionals and companies. Organizations must recognize that seemingly easy, fully automated solutions often lead to suboptimal results. And professionals, in turn, must invest in expanding their technical toolkit to remain competitive in this evolving landscape. Human capabilities, particularly in combining visual, semantic, and contextual pattern recognition, remain highly sophisticated. If you first analyze the text yourself and guide the AI system toward what truly matters, you can significantly improve the final outcome. In that sense, your role does not diminish. It becomes more strategic, more focused, and arguably more valuable.

Let’s be clear about what is happening: PMs who are weaker at design are doing work that designers are better equipped to do. That is a bad way to do things. Of course they can move faster when they ignore guidelines, systems, edge cases, and downstream consequences. The result is often a fragile house of cards. Sometimes that is good enough, but then the real issue is that the company does not need scalable or particularly sound design work. The issue is not AI. I also think designers moving towards the PM side can be valid. If AI speeds up execution, we can spend more time exploring the problem space and shaping product direction. So AI is not really replacing designers. It is enabling designers to move wider, towards both frontend and PM work. AI does not allow others to do our work better than us, while it can help us do UI work better than some developers and parts of product work better than some PMs. If design work is being replaced by sloppy AI output at a company, it probably means the company does not care enough about good design. Another frontend developer here. I'm suprised by how much your experience fits my own thoughts and conclusion, only in UX-language. The issue is what generative AI actually does: it generates a pattern that is _probably_ right, based on the statistical charateristics of similar patterns. That "probably" can never go away because that is what the process is based on. The first consequence of that is that you can never let generative AI go unsupervised because the chance of a mistake is always there. The second consequence is that you cannot _instruct_ AI in the conventional sense: you can only provide additional weights for the calculation, you can increase the probability of the correctness of an answer at an ever higher cost but you cannot reach 100% determinism. This is why you - or _any_ professional for that matter in their own domain - end up constantly saying that "hold on, let's validate that first". C-suite that drank the AI-koolaid see that as unnecessary bottleneck, but it's quality assurance that is absolute necessary unless you are willing to build up compounding technical debt. And this is why working with AI ends up being a soul crushing grind - if C-suite insists on using AI to amximize sales pitch-output, you end up with trying to get the harness right and reviewing in an infinite loop, using your job experience but without doing what your job actually is. The result is burnt out professionals and slop doomed to collapse. Will C-suite ever know better? Hard to say. My personal take is - and an increasing number of studies also indicate - that putting all the effort into generative AI simply isn't worth it.
